content: Ferric hydroxide, also known as iron(III) oxide-hydroxide, refers to a group of chemical compounds that are oxide-hydroxides of iron. These compounds can exist in either anhydrous or hydrated forms. The monohydrate form, often referred to as iron(III) hydroxide, is also known as hydrated iron oxide or yellow iron oxide. Iron(III) oxide-hydroxide occurs naturally in four polymorphic forms, denoted by the Greek letters α, β, γ, and δ. The α polymorph, goethite (α-FeO(OH)), has been used as a pigment since prehistoric times. The β polymorph, akaganéite, forms through weathering and has been identified in meteorites and on the lunar surface. The γ polymorph, lepidocrocite, is commonly found as rust inside steel water pipes and tanks. The δ polymorph, feroxyhyte, forms under high-pressure conditions on sea and ocean floors but is thermodynamically unstable at surface conditions, where it tends to convert to goethite. Additionally, iron(III) oxide-hydroxide can occur as siderogel, a colloidal form, and as limonite, a mixture primarily composed of goethite, lepidocrocite, quartz, and clay minerals. Goethite and lepidocrocite, both of which crystallize in the orthorhombic system, are the most common forms of iron(III) oxide-hydroxide and serve as the primary mineral carriers of iron in soils. Ferrihydrite, another related compound, is also a significant soil constituent. Pigment Yellow 42, derived from iron(III) oxide-hydroxide, is FDA-approved for use in cosmetics and is also utilized in some tattoo inks. The solid material exhibits a color range from yellow to dark brown and black. Iron oxide-hydroxide is further employed in aquarium water treatment as a phosphate binder. Recently, two forms of iron oxide-hydroxide nanoparticles have been identified as highly effective adsorbents for removing lead from aquatic environments. In chemical solutions containing both iron(II) and iron(III), ferric hydroxide precipitates at a pH range of 2 to 4, while ferrous hydroxide precipitates at a pH range of 7 to 9. This property is exploited in chemical analysis for the fractional precipitation of the two hydroxides. Ferric hydroxide can be synthesized by reacting ferric chloride with sodium hydroxide. Alternatively, iron(II) can be oxidized to iron(III) using hydrogen peroxide in the presence of an acid. The overall reaction involves the conversion of iron(II) to iron(III) hydroxide. Regarding safety, iron oxides are associated with specific risk and safety phrases, including R36 (irritating to eyes), R37 (irritating to respiratory system), R38 (irritating to skin), S26 (in case of contact with eyes, rinse immediately with plenty of water and seek medical advice), and S36 (wear suitable protective clothing).
